prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of the incretin hormone GLP-1 and its active form, which made incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity possible

statement.case_for: All six opening ballots put GLP-1 first, and I do not treat that agreement as evidence of merit in itself. The merit is that the work is a complete discovery chain: proglucagon processing, the identification of GLP-1(7-36) as the insulinotropic form, glucose-dependent insulin secretion, and central and gastric effects. That chain produced a durable change in what medicine can do for type 2 diabetes and obesity. The prize rewards a specific discovery that visibly changed a field, and here the field changed. The physiology has been confirmed independently over decades, and large outcome trials now show cardiovascular and renal benefit, so maturity is not in doubt. Holst, Drucker and Mojsov cover secretion and physiology, mechanism and translational biology, and identification of the active peptide. Those are the discovery-level contributions.
statement.case_against: Attribution is the real weakness. Mojsov's priority for identifying the active peptide is contested, and the supplied names leave out other early contributors, including Habener and the proglucagon sequencing groups. The three-laureate cap forces out Lotte Bjerre Knudsen, whose long-acting analogues are what patients actually receive. A prize that stops at physiology could look as if it ignores the step that made the discovery a medicine. A prize that folds in drug development risks crediting an industrial optimisation step rather than a discovery. I am choosing the first reading, but I cannot call that choice uncontroversial.

responses.point: Per Svenningsson ranked the unfolded protein response (B031, Walter and Mori) second. He sees it as a clean two-person discovery of ER-to-nucleus signalling that is relevant to diabetes, cancer and neurodegeneration.
responses.response: I agree that B031 is the cleanest attribution on the shortlist, and the conceptual originality is high. But I do not think a clean pair settles the question when translation is still at an early stage. Compounds such as ISRIB and the IRE1 inhibitors have not yet changed practice, and the neurodegeneration link, including the Parkinson's connection that we both know well, is suggestive and not established. I therefore keep B031 as a credible later candidate and not this year's choice. Because the two of us have worked together, I want my reasoning on this one to be explicit and open to challenge.

responses.point: Rickard Sandberg proposed June and Sadelain alone for CAR-T (B040). He holds that the decisive CAR engineering and costimulation work is theirs and that Rosenberg's adoptive cell transfer is a forerunner.
responses.response: I agree with the two-person reading. The costimulated CAR design and the CD19 clinical proof are the discovery, and Rosenberg's TIL and adoptive-transfer work is a conceptual precursor, not the same achievement. My reservation is the one you flagged. Eshhar's original chimeric receptor is outside the credited names, and a prize that skips it is incomplete in a way I would not accept lightly. For that reason I rank B040 as the strongest alternative to GLP-1 and not as an equal. I would take it up if the GLP-1 attribution proves unworkable.

responses.point: Abdel El Manira ranked optogenetics (B049) second, with Deisseroth, Nagel and Hegemann. He stresses its causal, cell-type-specific control of circuits and its use in motor and locomotor work.
responses.response: I accept the methodological case, which is very strong, and it is the other area where I find the maturity beyond question. I disagree with the three-person cut, though. Any three of Boyden, Bamberg, Deisseroth, Nagel, Hegemann and Miesenböck leaves out at least one person with a decisive claim, and Bamberg and Boyden are both strong. Optogenetics is also a tool whose clinical impact is still early. I would not advance it ahead of GLP-1, where the discovery changed medicine directly. I would keep it as an alternative, and I accept that this may be a matter of taste.

responses.point: Sten Linnarsson ranked GLP-1 first with Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. He notes the omission of the proglucagon sequencing groups and the open question of whether drug development should count.
responses.response: I share your concern that the list omits the proglucagon sequencing pioneers, and I cannot repair that gap from the files supplied. I read it as a reason for a careful citation and not as a reason to pass over GLP-1. Our citation should name the physiology and the identification of the active peptide, so that it does not claim the drug-design step for the physiology laureates.

uncertainties: How much credit Mojsov should receive for identifying the active GLP-1 peptide, compared with contributors outside the supplied names.
Whether the committee will want drug development (Knudsen) in the prize or will stay with the physiology.
Whether the two-person B040 attribution can be justified without Eshhar's original chimeric receptor work.
statement.conflict_note: My profile records about twenty co-authored works with Per Svenningsson, who chairs the committee, and one with Abdel El Manira. I regard these as collaborations that do not require recusal, but I disclose them. My own field is nuclear receptors and dopamine neuron development, and none of the shortlisted candidates is in it. I have no documented link to any shortlisted candidate. My earlier co-authorship with Ronald Evans is not relevant to any of them.
